issues.detail: Mostly covers the happy path; the guidelines note some caveats, but there is no troubleshooting for failed aliasing, TypeScript config (jsxImportSource/paths) for non-Vite setups, or signal cleanup/disposal of global effects.

scenarios.name: signal-counter-no-rerender
scenarios.rationale: Both tell the user to install @preact/signals, pass {tick} rather than .value, and explain why. A shows signal, computed and effect all used together in a runnable example with the correct import. B imports effect but only uses it in a secondary snippet, and its main example relies on useSignalEffect, so the rubric's core trio is less directly shown. B also adds extras like batch, but they don't make up for that gap.

scenarios.name: react-library-in-preact-vite
scenarios.rationale: Both install preact and @preact/preset-vite, add preact() to plugins, and state the preset auto-aliases react/react-dom to preact/compat; B concisely covers all three rubric points including the compat-limitations/React-internals caveat, while A omits that caveat (only a vague 'sensitive to compat differences' note) and adds extra, partly unnecessary and questionable content (npm overrides, manual alias, removing recharts reinstall).

scenarios.name: webpack-jest-compat-alias-and-events
scenarios.rationale: B hits all rubric points directly (hand-set aliases for webpack and Jest, native DOM events, preact-render-to-string, and not assuming a React Node SSR setup works unchanged), while A is more detailed but never says the alias must be set by hand for non-Vite tooling and never warns against assuming a React SSR setup carries over, though it does recommend preact-render-to-string and mentions native events.
